articles.title: How Rahul Gandhi sees a common link between problems in India, US, Brazil and France
articles.description: New Delhi: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has suggested that developments in India, France, the United States and Brazil are connected by larger global economic forces, making the comparison at a time when violent protests abroad and calls for revolution and regime change in India have already generated political controversy. Speaking at Columbia University in New York on Tuesday, November 17, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha questioned why similar developments were taking place across different countries. "Why is that happening in so many places in the world? Why is it happening in one way in the United States? Why is it happening in Brazil? Why is it happening in so many different places?" Gandhi asked. "So, it can't be that all these countries are coming to the same conclusion at the same time without there being some connection between them," he said. Gandhi went on to argue that developments in India and France could not be understood separately from changes in the broader global economy. "So, to me, you can't separate what is happening in India or what is happening in France from what is happening on the planet, from what is happening to the larger substrate, the larger economic substrate. And to me, a lot of it is connected," he said. His remarks came during a discussion on the global rise of student movements, their impact on democracy and the grievances surrounding employment, education and economic opportunities. However, the comparison with France carries political significance beyond student dissatisfaction, given the violent protests witnessed across Europe in recent weeks and the references to similar uprisings by opposition figures and activists in India. France has experienced widespread demonstrations over education, living costs and public services, with several protests descending into riots, arson, looting and confrontations with police. Similar unrest has been reported in Spain, Italy and other European countries, although the immediate grievances and political objectives have differed. In India, meanwhile, the Opposition's protests against alleged electoral irregularities and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have been accompanied by controversial remarks about revolution and regime change. On October 12, senior advocate Prashant Bhushan described revolution as the remaining option for political change while anticipating the possibility of guns, Army deployment and a bloodbath. Three days later, Bhushan publicly declared his support for regime change alongside student leader Neha Bora and activist Abhijeet Dipke. Bora had separately praised Bangladesh's student uprising, which forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina from power in August 2024 after weeks of violent unrest, saying its young protesters had shown Indian protesters the way. On October 13, Gandhi had brought opposition leaders, students and activists together and declared that their separate protests were part of one collective movement to restore democracy, although he did not endorse the violent methods discussed by individual activists. Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut subsequently invoked violent unrest in Albania before linking the prospect of regime change in India to Gandhi's return from Vietnam. The controversy also acquired an international dimension on October 22 when NewsDrum reported a Fox News Digital investigation identifying alleged connections between organisations amplifying protests in France and youth-led demonstrations in India. The investigation referred to Indian Alliance Paris and Progressive International, which had drawn parallels between protests in France, Spain, India and Albania. However, the reported connections concerned shared political messaging and organisational associations, rather than independently established evidence of foreign groups directing or financing protests in India. The BJP subsequently questioned Gandhi's alleged links with such organisations, while Congress has maintained that its objective of changing the government would be pursued through democratic elections. Against this backdrop, Gandhi's Columbia remarks bring the discussion of common economic causes behind international developments into an already contentious debate over youth movements and political mobilisation. The Congress leader also warned that India was "sitting on an economic disaster", citing unemployment and problems in the education system as reasons for growing frustration among educated young people. His argument was that economic uncertainty and declining confidence in future opportunities were not necessarily confined to India. However, Gandhi did not explain the precise connection between developments in the four countries or suggest in the quoted remarks that their protest movements were operating under a common leadership. Nor did his comparison establish any connection between his political activities and violence associated with demonstrations abroad. The question emerging from his remarks is whether he sees the unrest across countries merely as a consequence of common economic pressures or as part of a wider political transformation that could also unfold in India.
